springboot-ioc.tldr:
• The container creates and wires beans; use constructor injection so dependencies are final and explicit.
  • Stereotypes (@Service, @Repository…) are scanned; @Bean methods build third-party objects.
  • Resolve multiple candidates with @Primary, @Qualifier, or inject a List/Map of implementations.
  • @Configuration classes are proxied so inter-@Bean calls return the same singleton.
springboot-ioc.body:
Inversion of Control (IoC): your objects don't create or look up their collaborators; a container creates them, wires them together and manages their lifecycle. Dependency injection (DI) is how Spring implements IoC: dependencies are passed in (constructor, setter or field).

Without IoC, OrderService is welded to concrete classes and configuration; testing means real databases. With IoC it depends on interfaces, and tests pass fakes through the constructor.

How the container starts

Two phases matter: first Spring builds bean definitions (recipes), then it creates bean instances. Post-processors at each phase are how almost every Spring feature plugs in.

Injection styles

Java
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    private final PaymentClient payments;

    // Constructor injection: the recommended style. With a single constructor, @Autowired is optional.
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repo, PaymentClient payments) {
        this.repo = repo;
        this.payments = payments;
    }
}
Style Pros Cons
Constructor dependencies final (immutable, thread-safe), object never half-built, required deps explicit, plain new in unit tests, circular deps fail fast long constructors reveal too many responsibilities (a useful signal)
Setter optional dependencies, reconfiguration object can exist without its dependencies
Field (@Autowired on a field) short hidden dependencies, can't be final, needs reflection or Spring to test

Stereotype annotations — all are @Components picked up by component scanning (from the main class's package downwards):

Annotation Layer Extra behaviour
@Component generic —
@Service business logic none (documents intent)
@Repository persistence translates persistence exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy
@Controller / @RestController web handler mapping; @RestController adds @ResponseBody
@Configuration bean definitions CGLIB-proxied so @Bean methods return singletons

@Bean vs @Component: @Component goes on your own class; @Bean methods build objects you can't annotate (third-party classes) or that need construction logic.

Java
@Configuration
public class HttpConfig {
    @Bean
    public RestClient paymentRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder,
                                        @Value("${payments.base-url}") String baseUrl) {
        return builder.baseUrl(baseUrl).build();
    }

    @Bean
    public PaymentClient paymentClient(RestClient paymentRestClient) {   // depends on the bean above
        return new HttpPaymentClient(paymentRestClient);
    }
}

Interview tip in a @Configuration class (proxyBeanMethods = true, the default) Spring subclasses the class with CGLIB, so calling one @Bean method from another returns the same singleton from the container instead of creating a new object. In @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) ("lite mode", used by Boot's auto-configurations for faster startup) or in @Component classes, it's just a plain method call that creates a new object each time.

When several beans match a type

Java
public interface NotificationSender { void send(String to, String msg); }
@Component @Primary class EmailSender implements NotificationSender { /* default */ }
@Component("sms") class SmsSender implements NotificationSender { }

@Service class Alerts {
    Alerts(NotificationSender defaultSender,                        // @Primary wins: EmailSender
           @Qualifier("sms") NotificationSender sms,                // explicit by name
           List<NotificationSender> all,                            // every implementation
           Map<String, NotificationSender> byName) { }              // bean name -> bean
}

Optional or lazy dependencies: Optional<T>, ObjectProvider<T> (getIfAvailable, getObject for prototypes), @Lazy (inject a proxy that resolves on first use).

BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext: ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory with eager singleton creation (fail fast at startup), events, internationalization, environment/profile support, resource loading and automatic registration of post-processors. Applications always use an ApplicationContext.

springboot-scopes.tldr:
• Singleton is the default and must be stateless or thread-safe; prototype creates a new bean per lookup.
  • A prototype injected into a singleton is created once: use ObjectProvider or a scoped proxy.
  • Lifecycle: construct → inject → aware → post-processors → @PostConstruct → proxies → use → @PreDestroy.
  • Circular dependencies are forbidden by default since Boot 2.6; fix the design.

springboot-autoconfig.tldr:
• @EnableAutoConfiguration loads candidates from AutoConfiguration.imports across jars.
  • Conditions (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty) decide what applies; your own bean wins.
  • Starters bring dependencies whose presence triggers the matching auto-configuration.
  • Debug with --debug or /actuator/conditions.
springboot-autoconfig.body:
@SpringBootApplication = @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration) + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan.

Auto-configurations are processed after your own configuration, which is what lets @ConditionalOnMissingBean back off when you've defined your own bean.

Java
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)                    // only if JDBC is on the classpath
@EnableConfigurationProperties(DataSourceProperties.class)
public class MyDataSourceAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean                            // the user's own DataSource wins
    @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "app.ds", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
    public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) {
        return props.initializeDataSourceBuilder().build();
    }
}

Common conditions

Condition Matches when
@ConditionalOnClass / OnMissingClass a class is (not) on the classpath
@ConditionalOnBean / OnMissingBean a bean of that type does (not) exist
@ConditionalOnProperty a property has a value (or is missing, with matchIfMissing)
@ConditionalOnWebApplication servlet or reactive web app
@ConditionalOnResource a resource exists
@ConditionalOnExpression a SpEL expression is true
@ConditionalOnCloudPlatform running on Kubernetes, Cloud Foundry…

Starters are dependency bundles: spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, Jackson, Tomcat and validation support; their presence on the classpath is what makes the matching auto-configurations activate. The Spring Boot BOM (spring-boot-dependencies) pins compatible versions of hundreds of libraries.

Debugging auto-configuration

Shell
java -jar app.jar --debug                       # prints the CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT at startup
curl localhost:8080/actuator/conditions         # same, over Actuator
Text
Positive matches:
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'javax.sql.DataSource', ...
Negative matches:
   MongoAutoConfiguration:
      Did not match:
         - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class 'com.mongodb.client.MongoClient'

Exclude one explicitly with @SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class) or spring.autoconfigure.exclude=....

What SpringApplication.run does, end to end

Writing your own starter (asked at senior level): an -autoconfigure module with @AutoConfiguration classes listed in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports, @ConfigurationProperties for settings, conditions so users can override everything, and a -starter module that just depends on it plus the library.

springboot-config.tldr:
• Precedence: command line > env vars > profile-specific files > application.yml > defaults.
  • Prefer type-safe @ConfigurationProperties records with @Validated over scattered @Value.
  • Profiles and profile groups switch config per environment.
  • Keep secrets out of YAML: env vars, Kubernetes Secrets or a secrets manager.
springboot-config.body:
Where properties come from — highest priority first (simplified)

A higher source overrides a lower one key by key, so production can override only spring.datasource.url via an environment variable while everything else comes from application.yml. Relaxed binding maps SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL, spring.datasource.url and spring.dataSource.url to the same property.

YAML
# application.yml
spring:
  application.name: order-service
  profiles.active: ${SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE:local}      # default profile "local"
app:
  payment:
    base-url: https://pay.internal
    timeout: 2s
    retry:
      max-attempts: 3
---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: prod                  # multi-document file: this part applies only to prod
app.payment.base-url: https://pay.prod.internal

Type-safe configuration beats scattered @Value annotations:

Java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.payment")
@Validated
public record PaymentProperties(
        @NotBlank String baseUrl,
        @NotNull Duration timeout,                 // "2s", "500ms" bind to Duration
        @Valid Retry retry) {
    public record Retry(@Min(1) @Max(10) int maxAttempts) {}
}

@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationPropertiesScan                       // registers every @ConfigurationProperties record
public class OrderApplication { }

@Service
class PaymentGateway {
    PaymentGateway(PaymentProperties props) { /* props.timeout(), props.retry().maxAttempts() */ }
}
@Value("${x}") @ConfigurationProperties
Type safety / structure one value, string-ish typed, nested objects, lists, maps
Validation manual @Validated + Bean Validation at startup
Relaxed binding limited full
IDE metadata / docs no yes (spring-boot-configuration-processor)
SpEL yes no

Validated properties make bad configuration fail at startup (during a rolling deploy, the new pod never becomes ready) instead of at the first request that needs the value.

Profiles

  • Activate with spring.profiles.active=prod (env var SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE), several allowed.
  • application-{profile}.yml files or spring.config.activate.on-profile sections override defaults.
  • @Profile("prod") / @Profile("!prod") enables beans conditionally (e.g. a fake payment client locally).
  • Profile groups: spring.profiles.group.prod=prod-db,prod-kafka activates several at once.
  • Keep profiles about environment differences, not feature flags.

Importing extra config: spring.config.import=optional:file:/etc/app/override.yml, configtree:/etc/secrets/ (Kubernetes mounted secrets, one file per key), vault://, aws-secretsmanager: (with the matching Spring Cloud modules).

Secrets: never commit them to application.yml. Inject through environment variables, mounted Kubernetes Secrets, or a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager); see API & Security → secrets.

Inspecting what's effective: /actuator/env (mask secrets!) and /actuator/configprops show every property and which source it came from.

springboot-rest.tldr:
• Use nouns, proper methods and status codes; return 201 Created with a Location for creates.
  • Validate with @Valid and Bean Validation on request records.
  • Map exceptions centrally in @RestControllerAdvice returning ProblemDetail.
  • Request flow: filters → DispatcherServlet → handler mapping → interceptors → argument resolution → message conversion.

springboot-jpa.tldr:
• Default *ToOne is EAGER: make it LAZY and fetch explicitly.
  • N+1 queries: fix with join fetch, @EntityGraph, batch fetching or DTO projections.
  • Collection join fetch + paging paginates in memory; page ids first.
  • Turn off Open Session in View; use SEQUENCE ids and JDBC batching for bulk writes.
springboot-jpa.body:
The layers

Mapping an aggregate

Java
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)   // SEQUENCE allows JDBC insert batching; IDENTITY disables it
    private Long id;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)                        // *ToOne defaults to EAGER: always override
    @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id")
    private Customer customer;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<OrderItem> items = new ArrayList<>();       // *ToMany defaults to LAZY

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)                              // never ORDINAL: reordering the enum corrupts data
    private OrderStatus status;

    @Version                                                  // optimistic locking
    private long version;

    public void addItem(OrderItem i) { items.add(i); i.setOrder(this); }   // keep both sides in sync
}

Entity states and the persistence context

The persistence context is a per-transaction first-level cache: loading the same id twice returns the same instance, and at flush time Hibernate compares managed entities with their loaded snapshots and issues UPDATEs for what changed (dirty checking). That's why you don't need to call save() on a managed entity after modifying it inside a transaction.

Repositories

Java
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    List<Order> findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter(OrderStatus s, Instant after);   // derived query from the name

    @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.items where o.customer.id = :cid")
    List<Order> findWithItems(@Param("cid") Long customerId);                // fetch join

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"customer", "items"})
    Optional<Order> findDetailedById(Long id);                               // load graph without JPQL

    @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true)
    @Query("update Order o set o.status = :s where o.id in :ids")
    int bulkUpdate(@Param("s") OrderStatus s, @Param("ids") List<Long> ids); // bypasses the persistence context

    List<OrderSummary> findByCustomerId(Long id);                            // interface projection: only 2 columns
    interface OrderSummary { Long getId(); BigDecimal getTotal(); }
}

The N+1 problem

Fixes:

Fix How Notes
Fetch join join fetch o.items in JPQL one query; careful with pagination and multiple collections
@EntityGraph declare attributes to load same SQL effect, no JPQL
Batch fetching spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50 or @BatchSize lazy collections load in IN (?, ?, …) batches: N+1 becomes 1 + N/50
DTO projection select exactly the columns needed best for read-only views

Detect it: spring.jpa.show-sql (dev only), Hibernate statistics (hibernate.generate_statistics), a query-count assertion in integration tests, or traces showing dozens of tiny DB spans per request.

Pitfall join fetch on a collection combined with Pageable makes Hibernate fetch everything and paginate in memory (warning HHH90003004 in Hibernate 6). Page the ids first (select o.id from Order o ...), then fetch details for those ids. Fetch-joining two List collections at once throws MultipleBagFetchException.

Other must-knows

  • LazyInitializationException: touching a lazy association after the transaction (and session) closed. Fix by fetching what you need inside the transaction, not by enabling Open Session in View.
  • Open Session in View (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true by default) keeps the session and a DB connection bound for the whole web request, including JSON serialization. Turn it off: spring.jpa.open-in-view=false.
  • Batching writes: hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50, hibernate.order_inserts=true, hibernate.order_updates=true, and SEQUENCE ids (IDENTITY prevents insert batching because Hibernate needs each generated id immediately).
  • save() on a new entity with a pre-set id triggers a SELECT (Spring Data calls merge because it can't tell new from detached); implement Persistable<ID> or use a @Version field so isNew() works.
  • Use @Transactional(readOnly = true) for queries: Hibernate skips dirty-checking snapshots.
  • Large batch jobs: flush() and clear() every N entities so the persistence context doesn't grow without bound.

springboot-transactions.tldr:
• @Transactional works through a proxy: self-invocation and non-public methods bypass it.
  • Only unchecked exceptions roll back by default; caught exceptions commit.
  • REQUIRED joins; REQUIRES_NEW suspends and uses a second connection.
  • Keep remote calls out of transactions; publish side effects AFTER_COMMIT; use @Version or FOR UPDATE for contention.

springboot-aop.tldr:
• Spring AOP is proxy-based (CGLIB by default in Boot) and intercepts public method executions.
  • @Around advice can time, retry, authorize or log any annotated method.
  • Self-invocation and final classes/methods aren't intercepted.
  • Transactions, caching, security and async are all AOP under the hood.
springboot-aop.body:
AOP separates cross-cutting concerns — logging, metrics, transactions, security, retries, caching — from business code. Without it, every service method would start with the same ten lines of timing, auth checks and try/catch. Spring AOP weaves that behaviour in at runtime, through proxies.

Every advised call passes through a chain of interceptors wrapped around the real method, like layers of an onion. The order is controlled with @Order (lower = outer); @Transactional and @Cacheable are themselves just built-in aspects in this chain.

Vocabulary

Term Meaning Example
Aspect a module of cross-cutting logic TimingAspect
Join point a point where advice can run — in Spring AOP always a method execution PricingService.quote(..)
Pointcut an expression selecting join points execution(* com.shop..service.*.*(..))
Advice the code that runs, and when @Around, @Before…
Weaving linking aspects to targets Spring: runtime proxy; AspectJ: compile/load time

Advice types

Advice Runs Can change result / swallow exception
@Before before the method no (can throw to stop it)
@AfterReturning after a normal return; can read the value no
@AfterThrowing after an exception; can read it no (exception still propagates)
@After always, like finally no
@Around wraps the call; you call proceed() yes — can retry, cache, time, replace

A real aspect: timing + metrics by annotation

Java
@Target(ElementType.METHOD) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Timed { String value(); }

@Aspect
@Component
public class TimingAspect {
    private final MeterRegistry registry;
    public TimingAspect(MeterRegistry registry) { this.registry = registry; }

    @Around("@annotation(timed)")                      // binds the annotation instance to the parameter
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, Timed timed) throws Throwable {
        Timer.Sample sample = Timer.start(registry);
        String outcome = "success";
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();
        } catch (Throwable t) {
            outcome = t.getClass().getSimpleName();
            throw t;                                    // never swallow
        } finally {
            sample.stop(registry.timer(timed.value(),
                    "method", pjp.getSignature().getName(), "outcome", outcome));
        }
    }
}

@Service
public class PricingService {
    @Timed("pricing.quote")
    public Quote quote(Cart cart) { /* ... */ }
}

Pointcut expressions you'll actually write

Java
@Aspect @Component
class AuditAspect {
    @Pointcut("within(com.shop..service..*)")                       // any method in service packages
    void serviceLayer() {}

    @Pointcut("execution(public * *(..)) && @within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)")
    void publicServiceMethods() {}

    @AfterReturning(pointcut = "serviceLayer() && @annotation(audited)", returning = "result")
    void audit(JoinPoint jp, Audited audited, Object result) {
        auditLog.record(audited.action(), jp.getArgs(), result);
    }
}

JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB

JDK dynamic proxy CGLIB proxy
Requires an interface a non-final class with an accessible constructor
Inject as the interface type only the class or the interface
Can't intercept methods not on the interface final / private / static methods
Spring Boot default — yes (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true)

The self-invocation problem

Limitations recap: self-invocation isn't intercepted; final classes/methods can't be CGLIB-proxied; only Spring beans get proxies (new-ed objects don't); only method execution join points. When you truly need field access, constructor or non-bean interception, use full AspectJ (compile-time or load-time weaving).

Interview tip "How does @Transactional work?" — a BeanPostProcessor wraps the bean in a proxy after initialization; the proxy's TransactionInterceptor (an @Around advice) begins the transaction, calls proceed(), then commits or rolls back. Everything about its pitfalls follows from that one sentence.

springboot-security.tldr:
• Security is a servlet filter chain; authentication ends up in SecurityContextHolder.
  • Stateless APIs: disable sessions and CSRF, validate JWTs with the resource server support.
  • Method security with @PreAuthorize handles object-level rules.
  • 401 = not authenticated; 403 = authenticated but forbidden.
springboot-security.body:
Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters in front of DispatcherServlet. A DelegatingFilterProxy registered with the servlet container hands the request to FilterChainProxy, which picks the first SecurityFilterChain whose matcher fits the request and runs its filters in order.

Core objects

  • Authentication — principal (who), credentials, GrantedAuthoritys (what roles/scopes).
  • SecurityContextHolder — a ThreadLocal; with @Async or your own executors the context does not follow automatically (use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor).
  • 401 Unauthorized = not authenticated (missing/invalid/expired token); 403 Forbidden = authenticated but not allowed.

Resource server configuration (JWT bearer tokens)

Java
@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .securityMatcher("/api/**", "/actuator/**")
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())                 // stateless API, no cookies → no CSRF risk
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/v1/products/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/api/v1/orders/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers("/api/v1/orders/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(jwt -> jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(rolesFromClaim())))
            .build();
    }

    // Map a custom "roles" claim to ROLE_ authorities (default only maps "scope"/"scp" to SCOPE_)
    private JwtAuthenticationConverter rolesFromClaim() {
        JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter roles = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
        roles.setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles");
        roles.setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_");
        JwtAuthenticationConverter c = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
        c.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(roles);
        return c;
    }

    @Bean PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder(); } // bcrypt by default
}
YAML
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com/realms/shop
# Boot discovers the JWKS URL from the issuer, caches the public keys and validates: signature, exp, nbf, iss.
# Also validate the audience:
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences: order-service

Method security — for rules that depend on the data:

Java
@Service
public class OrderQueryService {
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #customerId == authentication.name")
    public List<Order> ordersFor(String customerId) { /* ... */ }

    @PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")     // checks the loaded object
    public Order get(Long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); }
}

@GetMapping("/me/orders")
List<OrderResponse> mine(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    return service.ordersFor(jwt.getSubject());
}

Pitfall URL rules alone don't stop IDOR (insecure direct object reference): GET /orders/42 by an authenticated user must still check that order 42 belongs to them. Do it in the query (findByIdAndOwnerId) or with @PostAuthorize.

The JWT login and request flow

JWT structure: header.payload.signature, each base64url-encoded. RS256/ES256 tokens are signed with the issuer's private key and verified with the public key from the JWKS endpoint, so services never hold a signing secret. The payload is readable, not encrypted: never put secrets or PII you wouldn't log into it.

Stateless JWT vs server sessions

JWT access tokens Server-side sessions (cookie + Redis/Spring Session)
Scaling no lookup per request shared store needed
Revocation hard — wait for expiry or keep a deny-list (jti in Redis) delete the session
Size larger headers tiny cookie id
CSRF not applicable with Authorization header needs CSRF protection
Best for APIs, service-to-service, mobile browser apps (BFF pattern)

Service-to-service: OAuth2 client credentials grant (Spring's OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager attaches and refreshes tokens on RestClient/WebClient), or mTLS inside a service mesh. See API & Security for OWASP risks, CORS and secret handling.

springboot-testing.tldr:
• Unit test logic without Spring; use slices (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) for layers.
  • Testcontainers with @ServiceConnection gives real databases and brokers in tests.
  • @MockitoBean (Boot 3.4+) replaces @MockBean; every distinct mock set creates a new context.
  • Keep the suite fast by reusing contexts.
springboot-testing.body:
The test pyramid for a Spring service

What each annotation loads

Annotation Loads Use for Typical time
plain JUnit + Mockito nothing business rules, calculations ms
@WebMvcTest(Controller.class) MVC infrastructure, controller, advice, filters, Jackson URL mapping, validation, status codes, JSON shape, security rules ~1 s
@DataJpaTest JPA, repositories, embedded or Testcontainers DB, rolls back each test custom queries, mappings, N+1 checks 1–3 s
@JsonTest Jackson + JacksonTester serialization contracts <1 s
@RestClientTest RestClient/RestTemplate + MockRestServiceServer outbound HTTP clients <1 s
@SpringBootTest the full application context wiring, end-to-end flows within the service 5–20 s

Unit test: no Spring at all (constructor injection makes this trivial)

Java
class PricingServiceTest {
    private final TaxPolicy tax = mock(TaxPolicy.class);
    private final PricingService pricing = new PricingService(tax);

    @Test
    void appliesTaxAfterDiscount() {
        when(tax.rateFor("DE")).thenReturn(new BigDecimal("0.19"));
        Quote q = pricing.quote(cartOf("100.00"), "DE", "SAVE10");
        assertThat(q.total()).isEqualByComparingTo("107.10");      // (100 - 10) * 1.19
    }
}

Web slice

Java
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
@Import(SecurityConfig.class)
class OrderControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean OrderService service;         // Boot 3.4+ (replaces deprecated @MockBean)

    @Test
    void returns404AsProblemDetail() throws Exception {
        when(service.find(99L)).thenThrow(new OrderNotFoundException(99L));
        mvc.perform(get("/api/v1/orders/99").with(jwt()))
           .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
           .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON))
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Order not found"));
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsInvalidBody() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/api/v1/orders").with(jwt())
                .header("Idempotency-Key", "k1")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("""
                    {"customerId": null, "items": []}
                    """))
           .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[*].field", hasItems("customerId", "items")));
    }

    @Test
    void anonymousGets401() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/v1/orders/1")).andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
    }
}

Repository slice against real Postgres

Java
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)   // don't swap in H2
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {
    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;
    @Autowired TestEntityManager em;

    @Test
    void findWithItemsUsesOneQuery() {
        // persist fixtures with em.persist(...), then em.flush(); em.clear();
        Statistics stats = em.getEntityManager().getEntityManagerFactory()
                .unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
        stats.clear();
        repo.findWithItems(1L).forEach(o -> o.getItems().size());
        assertThat(stats.getPrepareStatementCount()).isEqualTo(1);           // guards against N+1
    }
}

Full integration test with real infrastructure

Java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@Testcontainers
class OrderFlowIT {
    @Container @ServiceConnection                 // Boot 3.1+: sets spring.datasource.* automatically
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static KafkaContainer kafka = new KafkaContainer(DockerImageName.parse("apache/kafka:3.7.0"));

    @Autowired TestRestTemplate http;
    @Autowired KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafkaTemplate;

    @Test
    void placesOrderAndPublishesEvent() {
        ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> res = http.postForEntity("/api/v1/orders", validRequest(), OrderResponse.class);
        assertThat(res.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED);
        await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
               .untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(consumedEvents()).anyMatch(e -> e.contains(res.getBody().id().toString())));
    }
}

Context caching — why some suites take 10 minutes

Spring caches application contexts across test classes by configuration (annotations, properties, profiles, mock beans). Every unique combination of @MockitoBeans, @TestPropertySource or active profiles costs a new context. Standardise on a shared base class, avoid @DirtiesContext, and start containers once (static @Container or the singleton-container pattern).

Interview tip prefer Testcontainers over H2 — H2's "PostgreSQL mode" doesn't support FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, JSONB, partial indexes or the same locking behaviour, so tests pass and production fails.

springboot-production.tldr:
• Actuator: liveness/readiness probes, Prometheus metrics, runtime log levels; expose only what's needed.
  • Graceful shutdown finishes in-flight requests; set shutdown phase timeouts.
  • @Cacheable/@Async/@Scheduled are proxy-based; give @Async its own executor with MDC propagation.
  • Run @Scheduled jobs once per cluster with ShedLock or leader election.
springboot-production.body:
Production readiness map

Actuator endpoints

Endpoint Shows / does Expose publicly?
/health, /health/liveness, /health/readiness status for load balancers and Kubernetes yes (no details)
/info build version, git commit usually
/prometheus, /metrics metrics internal network only
/loggers read and change log levels at runtime secured
/threaddump, /heapdump diagnostics (heap dumps contain secrets and PII) secured / separate port
/env, /configprops effective configuration (masked by default in Boot 3) secured
/conditions, /mappings, /beans auto-config report, URL mappings, beans dev / secured
YAML
management:
  server.port: 8081                                # actuator on a separate, non-public port
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus,loggers,threaddump
  endpoint.health:
    probes.enabled: true                           # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness
    show-details: when-authorized
    group.readiness.include: readinessState,db,redis
  observations.key-values.application: order-service
  tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1                # 10% of traces
server.shutdown: graceful                          # finish in-flight requests on SIGTERM
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s
logging.structured.format.console: ecs             # Boot 3.4+: JSON logs

Liveness vs readiness

Liveness Readiness
Question is the process stuck beyond recovery? can it serve traffic right now?
On failure Kubernetes restarts the container removed from Service endpoints, no restart
Should include internal state only (livenessState) dependencies it can't work without (DB), warm-up done
Never include the database (a DB blip would restart every pod) slow optional dependencies

Graceful shutdown on a rolling deploy

Custom health indicator and custom metrics

Java
@Component
public class PaymentGatewayHealth implements HealthIndicator {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    public PaymentGatewayHealth(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; }

    public Health health() {
        return gateway.ping(Duration.ofMillis(300))
                ? Health.up().build()
                : Health.down().withDetail("gateway", "unreachable").build();
    }
}

@Service
class CheckoutService {
    private final Counter failed;
    private final Timer checkoutTimer;
    CheckoutService(MeterRegistry registry) {
        this.failed = Counter.builder("checkout.failed").tag("reason", "payment").register(registry);
        this.checkoutTimer = Timer.builder("checkout.duration").publishPercentileHistogram().register(registry);
    }
    Receipt checkout(Cart cart) { return checkoutTimer.record(() -> doCheckout(cart)); }
}

Keep metric tag cardinality bounded: tag by status or endpoint, never by userId or orderId (each unique value is a new time series).

Observation API (Boot 3) — one instrumentation call produces a metric and a trace span:

Java
Observation.createNotStarted("inventory.reserve", observationRegistry)
        .lowCardinalityKeyValue("warehouse", warehouseId)
        .observe(() -> inventory.reserve(items));

Caching

Java
@EnableCaching
@Configuration
class CacheConfig {
    @Bean
    RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer ttl() {
        return b -> b.withCacheConfiguration("products",
                RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig().entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10)));
    }
}

@Service
public class ProductService {
    @Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id", unless = "#result == null", sync = true)  // sync: one loader per key (stampede guard, per instance)
    public Product get(Long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElse(null); }

    @CachePut(value = "products", key = "#p.id")
    public Product update(Product p) { return repo.save(p); }

    @CacheEvict(value = "products", key = "#id")
    public void delete(Long id) { repo.deleteById(id); }
}

Choose the store: Caffeine (in-process, fastest, per instance — inconsistent across pods) or Redis (shared, network hop). Always set a TTL. Cache annotations are proxies too, so self-invocation skips them. See Redis → caching patterns for stampedes and invalidation.

@Async — runs the method on a separate executor and returns immediately. Requires @EnableAsync; return void or CompletableFuture<T>; same self-invocation limitation; exceptions from void methods go to an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler (otherwise they're just logged).

Java
@Configuration
@EnableAsync
class AsyncConfig {
    @Bean(name = "notificationExecutor")
    ThreadPoolTaskExecutor notificationExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        ex.setCorePoolSize(4);
        ex.setMaxPoolSize(8);
        ex.setQueueCapacity(500);                                         // bounded: never an infinite queue
        ex.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        ex.setTaskDecorator(new ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator());       // Boot 3.2+: copies MDC / trace context
        ex.setThreadNamePrefix("notify-");
        ex.setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true);
        ex.setAwaitTerminationSeconds(20);
        return ex;
    }
}

@Service
class Notifier {
    @Async("notificationExecutor")
    public CompletableFuture<Void> sendReceipt(Order o) { /* ... */ return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null); }
}

Java 21: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true makes Tomcat, @Async and scheduling use virtual threads (see Concurrency → virtual threads for pinning and pool-sizing caveats).

@Scheduled — @EnableScheduling; fixedRate (start-to-start), fixedDelay (end-to-start), cron (with zone). By default all scheduled jobs share one thread, so one slow job delays the rest — set spring.task.scheduling.pool.size. Jobs run on every instance: use ShedLock (a lock row in the DB / key in Redis) or leader election so a cluster runs a job once.

Java
@Scheduled(cron = "0 */5 * * * *", zone = "UTC")
@SchedulerLock(name = "expireReservations", lockAtMostFor = "4m", lockAtLeastFor = "30s")
public void expireReservations() { reservations.expireOlderThan(Duration.ofMinutes(15)); }

Startup checklist for a production service: graceful shutdown + preStop hook, readiness includes DB, liveness doesn't, actuator on a separate port, JSON logs with trace ids, Prometheus metrics with bounded tags, connection pool and HTTP client timeouts set, open-in-view=false, validated @ConfigurationProperties, container-aware JVM flags (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75).

qa.q: What is the difference between Spring and Spring Boot?
qa.a: Spring is the framework (IoC, AOP, MVC, data, transactions). Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top: auto-configuration, starters for dependency management, an embedded server (runnable fat jar), externalized configuration and Actuator, removing most boilerplate setup.

qa.q: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?
qa.a: @EnableAutoConfiguration loads candidate configuration classes listed in AutoConfiguration.imports across jars. Each is guarded by conditions (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty), so it only applies when the library is present and you haven't defined your own bean. The --debug condition report shows what matched.
Dependencies can be final, the object is always fully initialized, required dependencies are explicit, it's testable without Spring, and circular dependencies fail fast.

No. Singleton means one instance per container; Spring adds no synchronization. They're safe only if stateless (only final injected dependencies) or if their mutable state is thread-safe. Never store request data in fields of a singleton.

@Transactional is applied by a proxy wrapping the bean. A call from one method to another inside the same class goes through this, not the proxy, so the annotation on the inner method is ignored. Fix by moving the method to another bean, injecting the bean into itself (lazily), or using TransactionTemplate programmatically.

qa.q: Why doesn't my transaction roll back on an exception?
qa.a: By default only unchecked exceptions (and Errors) trigger rollback; checked exceptions commit. Also, if you catch the exception inside the method the proxy never sees it. Use rollbackFor = Exception.class or rethrow.

REQUIRED joins the caller's transaction (one atomic unit; inner failure rolls back everything). REQUIRES_NEW suspends the caller's transaction and commits independently, e.g. writing an audit row that must persist even if the business transaction rolls back. It uses a second DB connection, so beware pool exhaustion.

qa.q: What is the N+1 query problem and how do you fix it?
qa.a: Fetching a list (1 query) and then lazily loading an association for each element (N queries). Fix with join fetch, @EntityGraph, batch fetching (default_batch_fetch_size) or DTO projections, and detect it with SQL logging or query-count assertions in tests.

@Component is placed on your class and discovered by component scanning. @Bean is placed on a factory method inside a @Configuration class, used for third-party classes or when construction needs logic.

qa.q: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?
qa.a: @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody: every handler's return value is serialized into the response body (JSON) instead of being resolved as a view name.

qa.q: How do you handle exceptions globally?
qa.a: A @RestControllerAdvice class with @ExceptionHandler methods mapping domain exceptions to HTTP statuses, returning a consistent body — ideally ProblemDetail (RFC 9457). Log unexpected exceptions once, there.
Named sets of configuration and beans activated per environment via spring.profiles.active. Profile-specific files (application-prod.yml) override defaults, and @Profile enables beans conditionally.

qa.q: How would you run a @Scheduled job only once across 5 instances?
qa.a: Use a distributed lock: ShedLock (lock row in DB or key in Redis with lockAtMostFor), a Kubernetes CronJob instead of in-app scheduling, or leader election (Spring Integration's LockRegistryLeaderInitiator, Kubernetes leases). Make the job idempotent anyway.

Instantiate → inject dependencies → Aware callbacks → BeanPostProcessor before-init → @PostConstruct/afterPropertiesSet/init-method → BeanPostProcessor after-init (proxies created) → in use → @PreDestroy/destroy/destroy-method on shutdown.

qa.q: How does Spring Security process a request?
qa.a: The DelegatingFilterProxy hands the request to FilterChainProxy, which picks the matching SecurityFilterChain. Filters extract credentials (e.g. BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter), an AuthenticationManager validates them, the result is stored in SecurityContextHolder, then AuthorizationFilter checks access rules. Exceptions become 401/403 via ExceptionTranslationFilter.

qa.q: How do you make a Spring Boot app production ready?
qa.a: Actuator health probes (liveness/readiness), metrics with Micrometer/Prometheus, distributed tracing, structured logs with trace ids, graceful shutdown, externalized secrets, connection pool and thread pool tuning, timeouts on every outbound call, resilience patterns, open-in-view=false, database migrations with Flyway/Liquibase, and container-aware JVM memory settings.

qa.q: What is the difference between @RequestParam, @PathVariable and @RequestBody?
qa.a: @PathVariable binds URI template segments (/orders/{id}), @RequestParam binds query parameters or form fields (?status=PAID), @RequestBody deserializes the request body (JSON) via message converters.

qa.q: How does @Cacheable work, and what are its pitfalls?
qa.a: A proxy checks the cache by key before invoking the method and stores the result after. Pitfalls: self-invocation bypass, caching nulls or huge objects, missing eviction on updates, no TTL with the default simple cache, and cache stampede on popular keys (use sync = true for local caches or a distributed lock).

cheat.springboot-cheatsheet:
IoC container and dependency injection

  • The container creates and wires beans; use constructor injection so dependencies are final and explicit.
  • Stereotypes (@Service, @Repository…) are scanned; @Bean methods build third-party objects.
  • Resolve multiple candidates with @Primary, @Qualifier, or inject a List/Map of implementations.
  • @Configuration classes are proxied so inter-@Bean calls return the same singleton.

Bean scopes and lifecycle

  • Singleton is the default and must be stateless or thread-safe; prototype creates a new bean per lookup.
  • A prototype injected into a singleton is created once: use ObjectProvider or a scoped proxy.
  • Lifecycle: construct → inject → aware → post-processors → @PostConstruct → proxies → use → @PreDestroy.
  • Circular dependencies are forbidden by default since Boot 2.6; fix the design.

How auto-configuration works

  • @EnableAutoConfiguration loads candidates from AutoConfiguration.imports across jars.
  • Conditions (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty) decide what applies; your own bean wins.
  • Starters bring dependencies whose presence triggers the matching auto-configuration.
  • Debug with --debug or /actuator/conditions.

Configuration, profiles and properties

  • Precedence: command line > env vars > profile-specific files > application.yml > defaults.
  • Prefer type-safe @ConfigurationProperties records with @Validated over scattered @Value.
  • Profiles and profile groups switch config per environment.
  • Keep secrets out of YAML: env vars, Kubernetes Secrets or a secrets manager.

REST controllers, validation and global error handling

  • Use nouns, proper methods and status codes; return 201 Created with a Location for creates.
  • Validate with @Valid and Bean Validation on request records.
  • Map exceptions centrally in @RestControllerAdvice returning ProblemDetail.
  • Request flow: filters → DispatcherServlet → handler mapping → interceptors → argument resolution → message conversion.

Spring Data JPA and the N+1 problem

  • Default *ToOne is EAGER: make it LAZY and fetch explicitly.
  • N+1 queries: fix with join fetch, @EntityGraph, batch fetching or DTO projections.
  • Collection join fetch + paging paginates in memory; page ids first.
  • Turn off Open Session in View; use SEQUENCE ids and JDBC batching for bulk writes.

@Transactional: propagation, isolation and pitfalls

  • @Transactional works through a proxy: self-invocation and non-public methods bypass it.
  • Only unchecked exceptions roll back by default; caught exceptions commit.
  • REQUIRED joins; REQUIRES_NEW suspends and uses a second connection.
  • Keep remote calls out of transactions; publish side effects AFTER_COMMIT; use @Version or FOR UPDATE for contention.

AOP: proxies, advice and cross-cutting concerns

  • Spring AOP is proxy-based (CGLIB by default in Boot) and intercepts public method executions.
  • @Around advice can time, retry, authorize or log any annotated method.
  • Self-invocation and final classes/methods aren't intercepted.
  • Transactions, caching, security and async are all AOP under the hood.

Spring Security and JWT

  • Security is a servlet filter chain; authentication ends up in SecurityContextHolder.
  • Stateless APIs: disable sessions and CSRF, validate JWTs with the resource server support.
  • Method security with @PreAuthorize handles object-level rules.
  • 401 = not authenticated; 403 = authenticated but forbidden.

Testing Spring Boot applications

  • Unit test logic without Spring; use slices (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) for layers.
  • Testcontainers with @ServiceConnection gives real databases and brokers in tests.
  • @MockitoBean (Boot 3.4+) replaces @MockBean; every distinct mock set creates a new context.
  • Keep the suite fast by reusing contexts.

Actuator, observability, caching, async and graceful shutdown

  • Actuator: liveness/readiness probes, Prometheus metrics, runtime log levels; expose only what's needed.
  • Graceful shutdown finishes in-flight requests; set shutdown phase timeouts.
  • @Cacheable/@Async/@Scheduled are proxy-based; give @Async its own executor with MDC propagation.
  • Run @Scheduled jobs once per cluster with ShedLock or leader election.
